newsitem.title: USA: Fran leaves behind 22 U.S. deaths, massive flooding.
newsitem.headline: Fran leaves behind 22 U.S. deaths, massive flooding.

text.p: Rain-swollen rivers sent deadly floodwaters over their banks and hundreds of thousands of battered East Coast homes remained without electricity on Saturday as residents mopped up after Hurricane Fran.
Rescue officials blamed the storm for at least 22 deaths in the Carolinas, Virginia, West Virginia and Pennsylvania.
Most of the deaths were caused by flash flooding and up to 15 inches (37.5 cm) of rain rather than Fran's gusts of wind which reached 120 mph (193 kmh) when the hurricane hit late on Thursday.
Powerful tidal surges crumbled buildings along beaches and winds damaged neighbourhoods far inland before Fran was downgraded to a tropical storm as it hit Virginia on Friday.
Well over one million people in the Carolinas and Virginia remained without power on Saturday, with many told they could not expect their power to be restored in less than one week, officials said.
Although hundreds of utility crews were working to bring power back, some 1 million people lacked electricity in North Carolina alone, said a spokeswoman for the state emergency operations centre.

Mike Lowder, an emergency operations manager in rural Bladen County in southeastern North Carolina, said some of the 80 percent of residents estimated to lack power were having trouble adjusting to life without electricity.
"People are so used to watching television, that they're not used to talking and dealing with each other. They get irritable," he said. "It also might be because the beer's warm."

North Carolina and Virginia were declared major disaster areas by President Bill Clinton, making victims eligible for federal assistance, although the final cost of the damage might not be known for weeks.

Damage in the Raleigh area alone was estimated at more than $930 million and officials hinted the statewide total could exceed $1 billion. In Raleigh, 4,000 homes were declared uninhabitable because of severe flooding.

Thousands of people were still living in shelters, many of those without power. And some residents of hard-hit shoreline communities returned home for the first time on Saturday, finding homes collapsed into the sea and belongings scattered hundreds of yards (metres) from their doors.

"We've just been picking up our things, clothing, artwork, medicine," said Carolina Redding, 25, a resident of Topsail Island, north of Wilmington, North Carolina, as she loaded baskets with sand-covered belongings.
North Carolina Gov. Jim Hunt ordered 1,000 National Guardsmen and 1,400 state prisoners to help clean up the damage. "This is the worst storm we've had in a long, long time," he said.

Virginia officials said the famed Shenandoah River continued to rise on Saturday, creating some of the most severe flooding of rural communities in years. Near Washington, the Old Town district of historic Alexandria was evacuated late on Friday as the Potomac River flooded streets with more than three feet (one metre) of water.

The north fork of the Shenandoah River, which slices through Virginia's picturesque mountains, was expected to crest on Saturday at more than 35 feet (10.6 metres) at Front Royal. The river reaches flood stage at 15 feet (5 metres).
"This is some of the worst flooding we've ever had," said Janet Clements of the Virginia Emergency Services Department.
The remnants of Fran caused more misery on Saturday when it dumped more than six inches (15 cm) of rain on already saturated ground in Ohio, Michigan and Pennsylvania.
North Carolina officials confirmed 15 deaths linked to the storm, mostly from traffic accidents and fallen trees.

Among the fatalities was one of three Marines swept away by raging floodwaters at the height of the storm, the Wilmington Morning Star reported. Emergency workers found one of the two Marines who survived clutching the branches of a tree in six feet (1.8 metres) of water hours later.
South Carolina reported two storm-related deaths.

As the remnants of Fran crossed West Virginia, officials reported two deaths due to high waters. In Virginia, a woman drowned when her vehicle was overtaken by fast-rising waters and another body was found underneath a car after floodwaters receded, state officials said.
The storm largely spared western Pennsylvania, but a man was killed when his car skidded off a wet road, police said.
